projectDesc.p: Prototype of a Digital Scholarly Edition (DSE) of the proem to Book III of Lucretius' De rerum natura, developed for the examination in Digital Scholarly Editing: Theory, Methods, and Practice held by Prof. Paola Italia at the University of Bologna for the academic year 2025/2026, based on the critical text established by Marcus Deufert.

segmentation.p: The critical apparatus is encoded inline using the parallel segmentation method. The <lem> element represents the critical text established by Marcus Deufert (2019), while <rdg> elements record readings from the primary manuscript branches, the indirect tradition, and humanist or modern conjectures.

interpretation.p: The apparatus fontium is kept separate from the critical apparatus and records ancient source attestations (Aug.–saec. IX ex.) as provided by Deufert (Praef. §§ 40–46).
The apparatus ad versus iteratos tracks internal formulaic recurrences across the poem, distinguishing identical repetitions (=) from verbal and thematic similarities (~) (Praef. § 39).

normalization.p: Orthography follows the non-normalized practice of the archetype as preserved in Deufert's text (Praef. §§ 53–55), maintaining archaic spellings, unassimilated prefixes, and the non-distinction between vocalic and consonantal u.

person.note: German classical philologist and professor (born 1970); editor of the 2019 critical edition of Lucretius' De rerum natura.
English classical scholar and critic (1756–1801); editor of an influential edition of Lucretius published in London (1796–1797).
Italian classical philologist and textual critic (1923–2000); renowned scholar of classical reception and Latin textual transmission.
British classical scholar (active early 20th century); author of conjectural emendations to classical Latin poets, including Lucretius (1921).
Greek-Italian Renaissance poet and humanist scholar (ca. 1458–1500); produced major conjectural emendations in his working copy of Lucretius.
Swiss classical scholar and epigraphist (1787–1849); editor of Latin classical texts and philosophical treatises.
German classical and Germanic philologist (1793–1851); established the landmark stemmatic edition and reconstructed the archetype of Lucretius (1850).
English classical scholar and pioneering textual critic (1662–1742); composed marginalia and influential conjectures on the text of Lucretius.
Early Christian author, rhetorician, and apologist (ca. 250 – ca. 325 AD); preserves indirect quotations from Lucretius in his Divinae Institutiones.
Roman grammarian and lexicographer from Thubursicu (active early 4th century AD); quotes numerous poetic lines in De compendiosa doctrina.

lg.l: In the murk of our darkness, you, Epicurus, raised your blazing lantern
to show us the blessings of life.
And I follow you,
walking with confident footsteps the trails that you have blazed,
not to be your rival, but in admiration and love,
and happy to have your example to guide me. How could I think of competing with you? A swallow might as well vie
with swans, or a young kid on its wobbly legs presume to race
alongside a strong horse.
You are our father, our leader, our pioneer, discovering truths that you share with us.
You are our guide, and from your writings,
You are like one of those bees that goes out to find the flowers and then brings back word to the hive of where the sweet nectar is for them all.
So do we feed on your words
of perdurable gold that are worthy of everlasting life.
We begin to follow your thoughts, your arguments, and your reasons,
about the nature of things, sprung from a divine mind,
and our mind’s terrors abate, while the opaque walls of the world
open wide to exhibit the intricate actions and movements that go on all the time throughout the limitless void.
Through you, I see the gods in their tranquil dwelling places,
where no harsh winds ever blow, where no dark clouds approach with the threat of violent storms,
and it never snows or freezes,
but a gentle air surrounds them attendant on their pleasures,
and smiles in an expanse of bounteous light.

div.head: Index of Philosophical Keywords (lines 1–22)
div.p: Key concepts of Epicurean doctrine and Lucretian poetic imagery appearing in the proem to Book III.

sense.def: Light of Epicurean truth and scientific enlightenment. It opens the proem (line 1) in stark contrast to the darkness of human ignorance, and concludes the Olympian vision of the gods (line 22) radiant in an expanse of bounteous brightness.
Rational explanation and philosophical system of Epicurus. It loudly proclaims (vociferari) the physical nature of things, dispelling unfounded superstitious terrors through logical inquiry.
The void: one of the two foundational principles of Epicurean atomism alongside solid bodies. An intangible, infinite space through which matter moves, combines, and dissolves unceasingly.
The walls of the world: the visible boundaries of the cosmic sphere. Upon the revelation of Epicurean physics, these restrictive ramparts withdraw and fall away, opening the mind to infinite space.
